body:
OBSERVED 2026-08-15 while cutting v4.1.35.

`Publish cwasync plugin` failed on v4.1.34 and v4.1.35 — the two most recent
releases. It last succeeded at v4.1.33. Nothing surfaced this: the workflow is
release-triggered, so a red run sits in the Actions list where no release step
reads it.

State, all verified by cloning new-usemame/cwasync.koplugin:

- downstream main AND its v4.1.33 release tag both ship plugin content declaring
  version 4.1.32
- our repo declares 4.1.33 at tags v4.1.33, v4.1.34 and v4.1.35 (unchanged since)
- the ONLY difference between our plugin source and downstream is the version
  string, in _meta.lua line 8 and main.lua line 30

Mechanism. `scripts/publish-cwasync-plugin.sh` decides "is a publish owed?" by
rsyncing our source over a clone of the downstream repo and staging it. The
version string differs, so `publish_owed=1` on every release. It then requires
the source to declare the tag being published (`expected_version=${TAG#v}`),
which it does not — 4.1.33 against v4.1.34, then v4.1.35 — and exits 1.

It is self-perpetuating: the failure prevents the publish that would resync
downstream, so the next release fails identically. Every release from here fails
until the plugin declares that release's version.

Why the pre-tag gate misses it. `tests/unit/test_cwasync_plugin_version_bump_gate.py`
compares the plugin against **what our own newest release tag shipped**. Our
plugin is byte-identical across v4.1.33..v4.1.35, so it correctly concludes no
bump is owed and passes. The publish script compares against **what the
downstream repo actually ships**. The two gates use different baselines, so a
drift between our tagged plugin and downstream's content is invisible before the
tag and fatal after it — precisely the "costs a whole extra version" failure
#1433 was written to prevent, one baseline over.

Remediation, in order of value:

1. Bump `_meta.lua` and `main.lua` to the release version in the same pre-tag
   commit as VERSION and the changelog roll. That unjams it at the next release
   and resyncs downstream.
2. Give the pre-tag gate the publish script's baseline — compare against the
   downstream repo's shipped content, not our own tag — so the two agree.
   Network-dependent, so it may belong in a release-gate job rather than the unit
   suite.
3. Make the failure loud. A release-triggered workflow that fails silently is the
   same shape as the manual step it replaced.

User impact today is limited: no functional plugin change is stranded, since the
content is identical apart from the version string. The cost is that the next
release which DOES change the plugin will fail the same way, and Updates Manager
reads a version that disagrees with the release it came from.
title: KOReader plugin publish has failed on every release since v4.1.33, and the pre-tag gate cannot see why
